passages.t: Loving correction, a good wife, and a kind hand to animals
passages.happening:
The chapter opens bluntly: ‘Whoever loves discipline loves knowledge, but he who hates correction is stupid’ (verse 1). ‘A man cannot be established through wickedness, but the righteous cannot be uprooted’ (verse 3).

‘A wife of noble character is her husband’s crown, but she who causes shame is like decay in his bones’ (verse 4). ‘The wicked are overthrown and perish, but the house of the righteous will stand’ (verse 7).

‘Better to be lightly esteemed yet have a servant, than to be self-important but lack food’ (verse 9). ‘A righteous man regards the life of his animal, but the tender mercies of the wicked are only cruelty’ (verse 10). ‘The one who works his land will have plenty of food, but whoever chases fantasies lacks judgment’ (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 10 began at home and chapter 11 went to the market and the city. Chapter 12 comes back to the ground under the reader's feet: the farm, the animals, the marriage, the work of the hands, and the words spoken over all of it. The first verse says again, with almost comic bluntness, what the book has said since 1:7. Being teachable is the doorway to everything else.

A wife of noble character translates eshet chayil, the same phrase that heads the poem of 31:10-31 and that Boaz uses of Ruth. Chayil means strength, ability or worth. In a world where a household's good name was shared, a spouse's conduct was never only private. The same is true in the other direction, as the book's many words to husbands show.

Most Israelites farmed small family plots of grain, olives and vines and kept a few animals. Israel's law cared for animals: the ox was not to be muzzled while it threshed, and working animals rested on the Sabbath. Verse 10 says the righteous know the life, nephesh, of their animal. Character shows in how a person treats creatures who cannot speak for themselves. The wicked have a kind of mercy that is only cruelty, kindness that serves the self.
passages.later: Boaz uses the same words of Ruth: ‘you are a woman of noble character’ (Ruth 3:11). And the law shows the care for animals that verse 10 praises: ‘Do not muzzle an ox while it is treading out the grain’ (Deuteronomy 25:4).
passages.asks: The chapter says that loving correction is the start of knowledge. Ask how you respond the next time someone corrects you. And ask how you treat those who cannot repay you or speak for themselves, animals included.

passages.t: Words that wound, and words that heal
passages.happening:
This is the longest block on speech in the collection so far. ‘An evil man is trapped by his rebellious speech, but a righteous man escapes from trouble’ (verse 13). ‘The way of a fool is right in his own eyes, but a wise man listens to counsel’ (verse 15). ‘A fool’s anger is known at once, but a prudent man overlooks an insult’ (verse 16).

“Speaking rashly is like a piercing sword, but the tongue of the wise brings healing” (verse 18). ‘Truthful lips endure forever, but a lying tongue lasts only a moment’ (verse 19). ‘Deceit is in the hearts of those who devise evil, but the counselors of peace have joy’ (verse 20).

‘No harm befalls the righteous, but the wicked are filled with trouble’ (verse 21). ‘Lying lips are detestable to the LORD, but those who deal faithfully are His delight’ (verse 22). ‘A shrewd man keeps his knowledge to himself, but a foolish heart proclaims its folly’ (verse 23).
passages.hearers:
Israel's courts met at the city gate and relied heavily on witnesses. The law required at least two for a conviction and gave a false witness the penalty he had tried to bring on someone else (Deuteronomy 19:15-21). A truthful or a false witness could decide a man's life. The sayings about witnesses in verses 17 to 19 were not abstract.

The pictures are vivid and physical: words lying in wait for blood (verse 6), a sword thrust, a tongue that heals. Words can wound as surely as a blade, and they can mend.

Verse 16 is about restraint. The fool's irritation is on display at once. The prudent person lets an insult pass, not because he is weak, but because he will not let every slight start a fight.
passages.later: The psalm asks who may dwell with God, and answers, ‘He who walks with integrity and practices righteousness, who speaks the truth from his heart’ (Psalm 15:2). James warns how much harm a little word can do: ‘Consider how small a spark sets a great forest ablaze’ (James 3:5).
passages.hard:
Verse 21 says no harm befalls the righteous. How can that be true?

Taken as an absolute promise, the verse is contradicted by the rest of Scripture and by ordinary life. Abel was righteous and was murdered. Jeremiah was faithful and was thrown into a cistern.

Proverbs knows this. Its sayings describe how things tend to go in a world God governs: the wicked do fill their lives with trouble of their own making, and the righteous are spared much of the harm that folly and violence bring. That is a true pattern, not a guarantee against every sorrow.

Some readers note that the Hebrew word for harm, aven, often means trouble that comes from wickedness, so the saying may be narrower than it sounds: the righteous are not overtaken by the mischief the wicked stir up. Others read it in light of the whole Bible, where final harm cannot touch those God keeps, even through suffering and death (Romans 8:28-39).

Either way, the verse must be read as wisdom. It must never be used to tell a suffering believer that their trouble proves some hidden guilt. That is exactly the mistake Job's friends made, and God said they were wrong.
passages.asks: The tongue can pierce or heal. Ask whom your words wounded this week, and whether you could go back and mend it. And ask which insult you could simply let pass.

passages.t: Diligence, a good word, and the path of life
passages.happening:
‘The hand of the diligent will rule, but laziness ends in forced labor’ (verse 24).

‘Anxiety weighs down the heart of a man, but a good word cheers it up’ (verse 25). ‘A righteous man is cautious in friendship, but the ways of the wicked lead them astray’ (verse 26). ‘A lazy man does not roast his game, but a diligent man prizes his possession’ (verse 27).

The chapter ends on the two ways: ‘There is life in the path of righteousness, but another path leads to death’ (verse 28).
passages.hearers:
Forced labor in verse 24 is the word mas, used for the labor gangs Solomon raised for his building projects (1 Kings 5:13-14) and for conquered peoples put to work. A family that could not support itself might fall into debt and servitude. The contrast between ruling and forced labor was a real fact of life, not a figure of speech.

Verses 24 and 27 form a pair on diligence and laziness. The lazy man of verse 27 cannot even be bothered to cook what he has caught.

Verse 25 is one of the book's gentlest sayings. Worry is heavy, and a good word from someone else can lift it. That is no failure. It is one of the ordinary ways God lightens a burden.

The last verse is hard in Hebrew. Its second line can be read as a contrast, as the BSB takes it, ‘another path leads to death’. Or it can be read as a second positive line, that the way of righteousness is not death, which some interpreters take as a glimpse of life beyond the grave. Either way, the chapter closes on the two ways of chapters 1 to 9.
passages.later: The prophet speaks of the tongue God gives ‘to sustain the weary with a word’ (Isaiah 50:4). And Peter quotes a psalm about the same choice of speech and path: “Whoever would love life and see good days must keep his tongue from evil and his lips from deceitful speech” (1 Peter 3:10).
passages.asks: A good word can lift a heavy heart. Ask who near you is weighed down, and what good word you could give them today. And if your own heart is heavy, ask whom you could let speak a good word to you.
